Okay, so I'm trying to figure out which geologic process caused the formation of Mount St. Helens. I remember that Mount St. Helens is a volcano in the Pacific Northwest, and I think it's part of a chain of volcanoes called the Cascade Range. I've heard that the Cascade Range is related to tectonic activity, specifically subduction. 

Subduction is when one plate dives under another, right? So, I think the Juan de Fuca Plate is the one that's subducting beneath the North American Plate. That makes sense because the Juan de Fuca Plate is in the Pacific Ocean, and the North American Plate is the continent of North America. Where they meet is the Cascadia Subduction Zone, which includes the Cascade Range and Mount St. Helens.

Looking at the options given: A) converging boundaries, B) diverging boundaries, C) transform faults, D) rift zones. I know that converging boundaries are where plates move towards each other, which is exactly what's happening here with the Juan de Fuca Plate subducting. Diverging boundaries would be when plates move apart, like in the mid-Atlantic Ridge. Transform faults are where plates slide past each other, creating strike-slip faults, which isn't the case here. Rift zones are associated with divergence, so that's not it either.

So, putting it all together, the formation of Mount St. Helens is due to the converging boundaries where the Juan de Fuca Plate is subducting beneath the North American Plate. That points to option A as the correct answer.
